Many health systems, particularly in low- and lower middle-income countries (LMICs), are lagging in their progress in achieving Universal Health Coverage and delivering on the promise of Health for All, constrained by workforce shortages, fiscal ceilings, and inadequate outreach to those lacking basic and essential services. Stark inequities in coverage of services and in health status persist. Strengthening community health worker (CHW) programs provides the fastest and most cost-effective route for health systems to achieve their full potential. CHWs should become the backbone of primary health care (PHC) and the foundation of health systems. Evidence from more than a decade of national-scale experience demonstrates that CHWs who are appropriately trained, paid, equipped, and supervised can extend high-quality essential services to the last mile while improving the overall efficiency of the health system. We are at a point in time when donor strategies and private investment are captivated by the promise of digital health and artificial intelligence. The most reliable approach to saving more lives is still a paid, supported CHW empowered with digital tools. At the same time, the contraction of Official Development Assistance (ODA) creates both risk and opportunity. ODA must pivot from supporting services to catalytic capital: time-bound, matching investments that accelerate governments’ own proCHW policy. A “next generation” of CHW programs in LMICs would enable CHWs to visit every home monthly and provide a broad array of PHC services as a result of adequate remuneration and appropriate training, supervision, logistical support, and integration into the health system. This could yield a highly favorable economic return—through productivity gains from better health, reduced health-care expenditures, and pandemic-risk mitigation. A “next generation” of CHW programs is our best bet for accelerating progress in achieving Universal Health Coverage and Health for All sooner rather than later.

The study aimed to explore the predictive ability of academic emotions on cognitive engagement among Arab university students within the Green Line in Palestine. To achieve the study's objectives, a sample of (503) male and female students were selected using the available method. The Academic Emotions Scale and the Cognitive Engagement Scale were applied to them. The results showed that academic emotions were ranked as follows: academic enjoyment and pride ranked first with a high level, academic hope ranked second with a high level, academic anger and boredom ranked third with a medium level, academic shyness and anxiety with a low level, and academic despair ranked last with a low level. The results showed that the level of cognitive integration as a whole was within the medium level. The results also showed positive predictive ability for academic enjoyment, pride, and academic hope in cognitive engagement, and negative predictive ability for academic despair in cognitive engagement. The study recommended improving levels of positive academic emotions such as academic enjoyment, academic pride, and academic hope.

Artificial intelligence is now part of the conditions in which Australian students learn. In NSW public schools a purpose-built chatbot is available from Year 5, and outside school students meet systems that write, explain, flatter and keep them company. This paper argues that primary schooling cannot respond to that change through technological integration alone. The deeper question AI raises is not which tool to add, but how a school should spend students’ time and what that time is for. Drawing on current research on AI and education and on the Castlereagh Statement on AI in Australian education, the paper sets out a view of what primary education is for and derives from it a founding principle, ten principles and a working school design. The proposed PrimarAI day is the ARC Day: six sessions on ordinary NSW bell times, two each of Augment (AI-supported mastery practice in mathematics and English under a teacher’s supervision), Reason (screen-free learning with a teacher, as a class) and Create (real-world learning organised through five Cs). Because the order rotates through the week, each part takes its turn at the first session of the day, when students learn most readily. The ARC Day is the latest of many versions of this school and the first that an existing school could trial with a single class. Digital literacy is taught as a subject from Kindergarten, and assessment is built into the fabric of everyday learning with the aid of purpose-built technology.

Background The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) has impacted most aspects of life and sparked debate over its responsible use. Objective As higher education grapples with how to leverage AI's benefits while accounting for its potential detriments, it is necessary to examine how undergraduates use and perceive AI. Method A replication, following the same methodology as Golding et al., examined how college students’ use and perceptions of AI differ from those of a comparable cohort 2 years ago. Students were from the same five universities and were predominantly women, White, Hispanic, or Black. Results Familiarity and prevalence of AI use were higher, and perceptions of cheating were lower. Open-ended data on motivations for (not) using AI and perceptions of (not) cheating suggested that students conceptualize AI through a nuanced lens. Conclusions The use of AI has grown substantially. Many students view AI as an instructional aid to guide their learning and emphasize the importance of how AI is used when determining whether it qualifies as cheating. Teaching Implications Students’ largely positive perceptions of AI suggest that AI's use is not slowing. Educators face the challenge of how best to leverage AI to enhance learning while not facilitating cheating or overreliance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study examined the use of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in mathematics teaching in the second cycle of basic education in the Sultanate of Oman. A descriptive–analytical design was employed, and the study involved 244 mathematics teachers from South Al Sharqiyah Governorate. A 46-item instrument comprising four domains was developed, and its validity and reliability were verified using appropriate statistical procedures. The findings indicated that the overall level of AI application use in mathematics teaching was moderate. The domains of perceived importance and teachers’ knowledge of AI applications showed relatively low levels, whereas the perceived level of challenges was moderate. Statistically significant gender differences were found in the domains of AI application use, perceived importance, and knowledge of AI applications, with female teachers reporting higher mean scores than male teachers. No statistically significant gender difference was found in the challenges domain. The findings should be interpreted in light of the study’s geographical and participant-related limitations, as the study was restricted to mathematics teachers of Grades 5–10 in one governorate. Based on these findings, the study recommends developing specialized national training programs to enhance teachers’ technological competencies and strengthen their instructional practices in alignment with national and global digital transformation initiatives. Keywords: artificial intelligence applications, mathematics teachers, the second cycle of basic education, mathematics teaching, artificial intelligence in education.

We present the ultimate closure of the *Metaphysical Sphere* pentalogy by mapping a profound epistemological loop. The framework that originally began as an inquiry into human consciousness (*The Projective Qualia*) was abstracted into computer science to fix the volatile, next-token prediction limitations of Multi-Agent Systems (*Projective Latent Synthesis v1.0*). By resolving the rigid binarism of artificial architectures through the creation of the generalized **Dynamic Hybrid Paradigm (HybridMAS)**, a revolutionary feedback loop has been completed. What was refined to build better artificial intelligence has now returned to the human domain as a practical, clinical, and pedagogical methodology for a healthy and sovereign consciousness. This paper formalizes the **Dynamic Phase-Switching Model of Mind**, positioning mental health not as a static biochemical status, but as an active, trainable algorithm of dimensional elasticity capable of neutralizing systemic alienation and destructive geometric interference.

Purpose Drawing on the socially embedded model of thriving and the conservation of resources model, this study aims to investigate the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) awareness, seen as a hindrance stressor, and thriving at work. In particular, it explores how AI anxiety mediates this relationship and how self-efficacy moderates the mediating effect. Design/methodology/approach To securitize the study hypotheses, data were obtained from banking employees via an electronic questionnaire, yielding 320 valid responses. The proposed model relationships were assessed through partial least squares structural equation modeling and process analysis. Findings The results uncover that while AI awareness is not significantly linked to vitality, it is negatively correlated with learning. Furthermore, AI anxiety mediates the direct influence that AI awareness has on dimensions of thriving at work. In addition, self-efficacy acts as a buffer, mitigating the adverse indirect influence of AI awareness on thriving at work through AI anxiety. Practical implications This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and digital literacy programs, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change. Originality/value This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and revise their role descriptions, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change.

This study examines how personal competencies shape university students’ scientific writing skills and whether artificial intelligence (AI) use mediates that relationship. Drawing on self-regulated learning theory, self-determination theory, critical literacy theory, and technology acceptance research, an integrated model positioned self-regulated learning, intrinsic motivation, and critical literacy as personal antecedents of AI use, and AI use as a mediator of their effects on scientific writing skills. Using a cross-sectional survey design, self-report data were collected from 615 students at six Indonesian universities through purposive sampling stratified by educational level and gender and analysed with covariance-based structural equation modelling in IBM AMOS 24.0. The model fitted the data well (χ²/df = 2.309, RMSEA = 0.046, CFI = 0.943, TLI = 0.941). Self-regulated learning (β = 0.321), critical literacy (β = 0.311), and intrinsic motivation (β = 0.216) significantly predicted AI use (R² = 0.607) and also directly predicted scientific writing skills, with the full model explaining 92.8% of its variance. Bootstrapped indirect effects (5,000 resamples, 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals) showed that AI use partially mediated all three relationships. Permutation-based multi-group analysis showed no gender moderation, whereas educational level moderated the critical literacy paths. AI amplifies existing personal competencies rather than substituting for them.

This chapter explores the role of the Internet of Things (IoT) in advancing a sustainable future, addressing the environmental, economic, and social dimensions of sustainability. IoT technology has enabled smarter resource management, enhanced operational efficiency, and improved quality of life across diverse sectors. This chapter examines IoT applications in environmental conservation, such as smart cities, energy management, and precision agriculture, which contribute to reducing resource consumption and carbon emissions. Economic sustainability is also discussed through the lens of IoT’s impact on industrial processes, supply chain optimization, and the circular economy, highlighting its potential to drive cost savings and reduce waste. Furthermore, innovations in healthcare, education, and public safety demonstrate IoT’s role in social sustainability by enhancing accessibility and resilience. Alongside these benefits, this chapter addresses the challenges that accompany IoT adoption, including data privacy, security, and the need for robust infrastructure and standards. The chapter concludes by exploring future advancements, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and 5G integration, and the policy frameworks necessary for IoT to fully realize its potential in enabling sustainable development. Through this comprehensive overview, the chapter emphasizes IoT’s capacity to drive meaningful change and advocates for ongoing innovation and collaboration to create a more sustainable future.

Occupational Health and Safety is an important component of higher education governance, as workplace risks include physical, administrative, psychosocial, ergonomic, and environmental risks. This study aimed to examine the relationship between Strategic Leadership and OHS, directly and through TQM as a mediating variable at STIH Adhyaksa. A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among 79 lecturers, administrative staff, and institutional leaders using total sampling. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analyzed using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS 4. Path coefficients, p-values, R², and indirect effects were assessed. Strategic Leadership was positively and significantly associated with OHS (β = 0.797; p < 0.001) and TQM (β = 0.933; p < 0.001). TQM was positively but not significantly associated with OHS (β = 0.072; p = 0.773). The model explained 87.0% of TQM variance (R² = 0.870) and 74.8% of OHS variance (R² = 0.748). The indirect relationship between Strategic Leadership and OHS through TQM was not significant (β = 0.067; p = 0.775). Strategic Leadership was positively associated with OHS, while TQM was not significantly associated with OHS and did not mediate the relationship. Research findings indicate that strengthening OHS at STIH Adhyaksa requires prioritization through strategic leadership, specifically regarding policy formulation, resource allocation, oversight, and the reinforcement of a safety culture. TQM needs to be more specifically integrated with the OHS system through risk identification and control, training, incident reporting, and continuous safety evaluation and improvement. The study contributes empirical evidence on the integration of leadership, quality management, and OHS in a legal higher education institution
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The physical learning environment, often referred to as 'the third teacher', exerts a profound, pervasive and measurable influence on the cognitive, emotional, social and even physiological processes of students and educators. This chapter aims to explore in depth, through an interdisciplinary perspective that integrates cognitive neuroscience, environmental psychology, architecture, pedagogy, ergonomics and health sciences, the multiple mechanisms through which the design, management and perception of educational spaces can significantly promote, mediate or hinder learning and overall wellbeing. The systematic analysis focuses on sensory and physical-chemical factors such as natural and artificial lighting, acoustic quality, microclimate (temperature, humidity, air quality), furniture ergonomics, spatial layout and flexibility, presence and integration of natural elements (biophilia), colour and aesthetic quality. For each of these domains, based on an extensive review of international scientific literature from the last twenty years, the direct and indirect effects on brain functioning are highlighted, with particular attention to the balance between limbic systems (amygdala, hippocampus) and prefrontal cortical regions, the modulation of neuroendocrine stress, and the optimisation of cognitive load.

The relevance of this topic stems from the need for a doctrinal analysis of the ethical and legal issues surrounding the use of artificial intelligence technologies in criminal proceedings. The purpose of this study was to examine the issues surrounding the use of artificial intelligence from the perspective of adherence to the principles of professional ethics by the parties and participants in criminal proceedings. Achieving this objective was made possible through the use of a range of methods, including dialectical analysis (to identify ethical and legal dilemmas) and comparative legal analysis (to study international experience), as well as methods of analysis and observation (to examine judicial practice and identify problematic aspects of the use of artificial intelligence technologies by the parties and participants in criminal proceedings), description (to document the research findings), and generalization (to formulate conclusions based on the research results). Three areas of artificial intelligence use in criminal proceedings have been identified that are controversial from the perspective of compliance with professional ethics by the parties and participants in criminal proceedings, specifically: 1) the use of artificial intelligence in criminal procedural documents; 2) the use of artificial intelligence in the presentation of evidence in criminal proceedings; 3) the use of artificial intelligence to predict the commission of criminal offenses. It has been established that the use of artificial intelligence technologies in criminal procedure documents is permitted when preparing document templates, processing information or analytical data, and searching for case law. However, the use of artificial intelligence technologies to formulate a legal position in a case contradicts the principles of professional ethics, in particular independence, competence, good faith, and confidentiality. It is argued that artificial intelligence-generated conclusions regarding the assessment of the risk of reoffending are of an auxiliary nature, and that the unethical use of artificial intelligence technologies in the presentation of evidence in criminal proceedings poses risks of violating human rights enshrined in international conventions, as well as of evidence being deemed inadmissible. The conclusions emphasize the need to develop ethical standards for the use of artificial intelligence technologies in criminal proceedings.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is reshaping education through new tools, and through new cognitive, relational and affective conditions. Artificial intelligence now selects content, suggests pathways, generates responses, personalises learning and influences the relationship between learners, knowledge and educational environments. This paper examines this transformation, asking what AI can do, and how it changes the ways in which people feel, learn, participate and recognise themselves in digital spaces. For many years, educational reflection on digital technologies focused mainly on Digital Literacy, understood as the ability to access, evaluate, produce and share information in technologically mediated contexts (Rivoltella, 2008). This is no longer enough. AI systems do not only organise information; they also affect motivation, trust, belonging, autonomy, dependence, responsibility and cooperation (Floridi, 2022). For this reason, the contribute argues for a shift from Digital Literacy to Digital Affective Literacy: a broader competence that includes the emotional, ethical and intersubjective dimensions of mediated educational experience (UNESCO, 2023). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 198-200. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.

The education of emotional intelligence becomes central within formal contexts insofar as it concerns the formation of subjects capable of recognising themselves, others, and the relational fabric of human experience. Children and adolescents are growing up amid affective precariousness, the fragility of adult presence, and the increasing technological mediation of interpersonal exchanges. In this scenario, human agency risks being obscured by practices that transfer to intelligent machines functions of listening, guidance, and consolation. The shift from embodied relationship to artificial interaction represents a critical juncture in contemporary education. Although young people are aware that chatbots, voice assistants, and Emotion AI systems possess neither consciousness nor authentic emotional participation, they increasingly entrust such devices with their insecurities and their need for recognition. The machine appears available, patient, and non-judgemental; for this reason, it is perceived as an interlocutor when adult relationships capable of genuine listening are lacking. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 63-64. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Generative AI and New Narratives of the Self.

Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.

Image-based dietary assessment can automate initial food logging, but meal photographs often leave food identity, hidden ingredients, preparation, and portion uncertain, making correction a recurring part of use. We introduce Human-AI Collaborative Correction, which reframes correction as communicate intent $\rightarrow$ regenerate $\rightarrow$ verify: users express what should change through text, voice, or guided clarification, the AI regenerates the linked dietary record, and users verify the result. In a within-participant study with 30 participants, compared with conventional Manual Search-and-Edit Correction, collaborative correction was associated with lower workload (Raw TLX: 35.83 vs. 55.00; p < .001), 21.0% lower recorded usage time, 51.1% fewer recorded clicks, and more favorable user-experience ratings; 90.0% preferred it overall. An exploratory nutrient analysis also found lower energy MAE. These findings support intent-driven regeneration as a promising interaction pattern for reducing correction burden while preserving user verification and making image-based dietary tracking easier to sustain.

Recent advances in embodied artificial intelligence have enabled robot manipulation agents to transition from executing static policies to autonomously constructing reusable skills, programs, and behavioral artifacts. However, successful execution, retained utility, and repeatable acquisition support fundamentally different empirical claims. This mechanism-oriented analysis critically examines 162 purposively selected primary studies through two complementary questions: how agent decisions reach robot control, and how capabilities are acquired and retained. We connect reported gains to their underlying artifacts, recipients, comparators, and evaluation boundaries. Retained programs and guidance can improve skill selection, command formulation, and recovery without altering the underlying actor, whereas neural adaptation and retention mechanisms govern distinct system components. However, aggregate performance gains can mask condition-specific losses or complete task failures. Applying our proposed five-level capability framework reveals that while intermediate levels of modular and simulation-based retention are widespread, no inspected system satisfies the Level-5 criterion of autonomous physical self-improvement under rigorous human- and procedural-intervention accounting. Although repeatable acquisition, transfer, and retention co-occur in bounded simulation under stated interaction budgets, independently verified hardware self-improvement with connected transfer, retention, and full physical cost accounting remains unresolved. These findings motivate standardized evaluation protocols that explicitly couple retained capability gains with repeatable acquisition and rigorous intervention-cost accounting.

Shape-memory alloys (SMAs) offer low mass, compact integration, quiet operation, and high work density, but their hysteresis and coupled thermal–mechanical behavior complicate repeatable control. This study develops a modular architecture in which natural-language command interpretation is separated from motion-profile generation and from actuator-specific models and controllers. The implemented pilot path was evaluated on a five-servo robotic hand, while the common comparison layer defines interfaces for technology-specific numerical models reserved for the next implementation stage. A locally executed large language model (LLM) converted user commands into port:angle pairs, and the same semantic front-end was coupled to either a fixed-step or zero-order Sugeno motion-profile generator. The semantic layer was evaluated using 60 recorded commands: 27 supported commands and 33 commands requiring rejection. Exact target generation was obtained in 25 of 27 supported cases (92.6%), while 17 of 33 invalid or unsupported commands were correctly rejected (51.5%), giving a strict overall result of 42 of 60 cases (70.0%). Direct observation confirmed the expected physical outcome in 23 of 27 supported cases (85.2%). The mean local response time was 25.30 s, the median was 16.71 s, and the 95th percentile was 66.73 s, confirming that the LLM is suitable only for the supervisory semantic layer. Because the pilot setup did not use an external position sensor, the fuzzy module is interpreted as a command-profile generator rather than a closed-loop position controller. The results validate the layered interface and establish an experimental and computational basis for a subsequent quantitative comparison of SMA and servo actuation.

Automated skin disease diagnosis remains a significant challenge due to inherent variations in skin tone, texture, lighting, and occlusions such as hair. Addressing these diagnostic difficulties is vital for developing reliable clinical decision-support systems. This research presents an automated classification framework utilizing deep learning, transfer learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The study utilizes the ISIC 2019 dataset, comprising images across eight diagnostic categories, including Melanoma, Nevi, and Keratosis. Six state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures—Xception, DenseNet169, EfficientNetV2S, MobileNetV2, InceptionResNetV2, and ResNet101V2—were fine-tuned and evaluated. The workflow integrates advanced preprocessing, comprehensive model training, and XAI-based validation to ensure transparency in diagnostic predictions. Quantitative evaluation reveals that Xception and EfficientNetV2S outperformed other architectures, achieving near-optimal performance, with Xception reaching an area under the curve (AUC) of 100% and superior scores across all primary metrics. Conversely, MobileNetV2 demonstrated the lowest comparative efficacy, with an accuracy of 62.66% and an AUC of 78.10%. The integration of high performing CNNs with XAI techniques provides an accurate, interpretable, and scalable solution for dermatological diagnostics. This approach not only improves classification precision but also enhances clinical trust by providing visual explanations for model decisions.

The study analyzes the impact of artificial intelligence on the assessment system in IT education, identifies its potential and risks, and provides recommendations for modernizing evaluation practices. Key areas of transformation have been specified: automation of code verification and personalization of learning through the generation of diagnostic materials; analysis of Git history and code; a methodology for documenting interaction with artificial intelligence in course and final qualification works. A hybrid knowledge assessment model has been proposed and tested.

Automatically reproducing Android app crashes from textual bug reports is challenging, particularly when the reports are incomplete and modern UIs exhibit high combinatorial complexity. Approaches relying on reinforcement learning or large language models (LLMs) struggle to infer missing steps and reconstruct user action sequences in vast UI interaction spaces. We present TreeMind, which integrates LLMs with an adapted Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for strategic UI exploration in bug reproduction. TreeMind formulates the reproduction as a target-driven search problem and leverages MCTS to iteratively refine action sequences. To enhance MCTS with semantic reasoning, we introduce two LLM-guided agents: Expander generates promising actions based on the current UI state and exploration history, while Simulator estimates the likelihood that each candidate action leads toward successful reproduction using dynamic environment feedback. With multi-modal UI inputs and tailored prompts, TreeMind performs feedback-aware navigation that identifies essential user actions and incrementally reconstructs reproduction paths. We evaluate TreeMind on 100 Android bug reports, including 90 from three benchmarks and 10 from GitHub. Experimental results show that it outperforms four state-of-the-art baselines in reproduction success rate and average time cost over all runs, suggesting the promise of integrating LLM reasoning with MCTS-based planning for automated bug reproduction.

As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly multilingual, distinguishing human-written from AI-generated text is essential for maintaining information integrity. However, research remains English-centric, with limited benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi. To address this gap, we introduce SHAKTI, a large-scale Hindi benchmark covering four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations. We evaluate its quality through human annotation and analyze linguistic, grammatical, and sentiment-based differences between human- and AI-generated texts. Building on these findings, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation-based detection framework with three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold), and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression using multi-distance RTT features). TRIDENT leverages semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated texts to identify AI-generated content. Extensive experiments show that TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. Further evaluations across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs demonstrate its multilingual applicability and robustness, while highlighting sensitivity to the translation model.

Abstract Background While AI has existed for decades, the introduction of generative AI tools and subsequent advancements in their capability and public use resulted in a shift in public awareness and perceptions of AI. In response, the research community has grown increasingly interested in understanding public perceptions of AI use in various contexts, including health care. Public perceptions shape AI acceptance and consequently integration into health care. It is thus crucial to understand public trust in AI and perceptions of risk as we consider its implementation moving forward. Objective This study aimed to (1) document the extent of what is known within the literature regarding public perceptions of AI applications in health; (2) interrogate existing definitions and theories of trust being used to guide investigations of public trust in AI; and (3) identify practice and policy considerations and support the design, deployment, and regulation of these technologies in a manner that is trustworthy. Methods The Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines were used to review publications between 2022 and 2024 across 4 databases, resulting in the inclusion of 41 papers for review. Key findings were then charted and organized into tables to help answer the proposed research questions. Results Public trust in AI in health care was shaped by discourse relating to AI performance and concerns related to depersonalization, loss of human connection, privacy, bias, and transparency. Trust was found to be higher when AI was supporting rather than replacing health care professionals and was influenced by emotional responses, anthropomorphism, demographic factors, and institutional trust. Furthermore, trust extended beyond algorithms to software interfaces, providers, developers, and governing institutions, highlighting the importance of governance and oversight. Conceptualizations of trust varied widely, and trust was defined through vulnerability, competence, benevolence, and integrity. Different theories identified suggested that trust operates across individual, social, institutional, and technological levels. Finally, trust was closely linked to risk and uncertainty, where perceived risk reduced acceptance, while AI literacy, transparency, and explainability mitigated concerns and fostered trust. Conclusions Trust in AI is not uniform, and as such, efforts to build and measure trust must account for these nuances to effectively mitigate risk and support informed, ethical AI integration and deployment. On the basis of the findings of this review, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that provides a general understanding of public trust in AI within a health care context that may guide research and policy and practice considerations. Our findings highlight the importance of considering public trust when implementing AI in health care and may support AI communication strategies, policy development, and trustworthy AI development.

documents.abstract: People must navigate socially transmitted information that varies from accurate to misleading or false. Here, we examined how perceived and objective truth predict belief change across three studies. In Study 1, four web-enabled frontier large language models (LLMs) and 200 human raters evaluated claims from two fact-checked datasets. LLMs outperformed humans in inter-rater agreement and discriminative sensitivity, supporting their use as a scalable proxy for objective truth. In Study 2 and 3, we applied this proxy to two large message corpora and examined its association with belief change. Perceived truth and LLM-derived objective truth independently predicted belief change. Moreover, objective truth moderated the association between perceived truth and belief change: the association between perceived truth and belief change was strongest for messages with lower objective truth and weakened as objective truth increased. These findings suggest that belief change reflects both subjective truth evaluations and the correspondence of information with reality.

Generative artificial intelligence enables users to produce text, images, music and software through processes in which human contributions vary considerably. This creates uncertainty about copyright protection and commercial ownership in Uganda. This article examines the Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Act, Cap 222, as amended in May 2026, alongside Ugandan copyright decisions, international instruments and selected comparative authorities. It adopts a qualitative doctrinal and comparative methodology, distinguishing the eligibility of an output for protection from the allocation and enforcement of any rights that subsist. The analysis finds that Uganda's framework can accommodate original human expression created with technological assistance, but does not expressly resolve the status of output produced without an identifiable human expressive contribution. The statutory treatment of employers and commissioning parties cannot safely be treated as an automatic entitlement to copyright in every machine output. Further uncertainty concerns the evidential treatment of prompts, the scope of protection in mixed works, contractual overstatement of ownership, moral rights and the relationship between output protection and infringement. The article proposes a contribution-based assessment that identifies the claimed expression, traces human decisions embodied in it, determines the scope of protection and then addresses ownership and third-party rights. It recommends targeted statutory clarification, practical guidance from the Uganda Registration Services Bureau, proportionate evidence preservation and improved contractual drafting. The preferred approach protects demonstrable human authorship while requiring evidence before any new exclusive right is introduced for substantially autonomous output.

Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a flexible computational approach for modeling social interactions among heterogeneous agents. This paper develops a novel framework towards characterizing and understanding LLM-based population-level bargaining of shared road space between autonomous vehicle (AV) and human-driven vehicle (HV) agents in mixed-autonomy traffic. Through controlled experiments varying traffic density, agent objectives, and traffic-domain knowledge, we first characterize bargaining outcomes and observe heterogeneous agreement rates across different experimental conditions. To understand how the bargaining process shapes the outcomes, we introduce a behavioral taxonomy that jointly characterizes numerical bidding actions and communicative attitudes. We examine two complementary aspects of social interaction: inter-agent bargaining dynamics and private-to-public behavioral transformation. Results reveal distinct interaction patterns associated with agreement and breakdown, including greater constructive reciprocity in agreement trials and more frequent conflict escalation in breakdown trials. Furthermore, private and public communicative attitudes often differ even when numerical bids remain unchanged. These findings illustrate how LLM-based bargaining simulations can support a structured analysis of social interaction behaviors in mixed-autonomy traffic.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems into the higher education landscape has triggered a global epistemological, ethical, and methodological debate (Crompton & Burke, 2023). If, on the one hand, technological innovation offers unprecedented tools for the optimization of teaching-learning processes, on the other hand, it raises profound cultural and pedagogical resistance within the academic community. The most deep-rooted concern in the scientific literature lies in the latent risk of a "dehumanization" of teaching, i.e. in a progressive and uncritical mechanization of the evaluative act that threatens to reduce the student to a mere cluster of quantifiable data (Selwyn, 2019; Williamson, 2017). Evaluation, historically understood as a fundamental relational, axiological, heuristic and interpersonal device between teacher and learner, risks being perceived as an alienating and aseptic process when it is mediated by complex algorithms of massive computation. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 334-340. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The ageing population has increased the need for built environments that support independent mobility, spatial orientation, and inclusive participation. Although Universal Design (UD) has advanced accessibility in the built environment, its application in vertical religious architecture is often discussed primarily through barrier-free and technical provisions. This study examines how selected UD principles are expressed in the architectural design of Tamkang Church, Taiwan, and how these architectural characteristics may support accessibility within a vertically organised religious environment. A qualitative descriptive-analytical approach was applied through a single-case study of Tamkang Church. The analysis used published architectural documentation, including drawings, floor plans, sections, circulation diagrams, photographs, project descriptions, and relevant literature. These secondary sources were examined thematically using three selected UD principles: Intuitive Use, Perceptible Information, and Low Physical Effort. The analysis suggests that accessibility in Tamkang Church is expressed not only through barrier-free facilities but also through spatial hierarchy, circulation organisation, environmental cues, natural lighting, material differentiation, and ergonomic elements. These features may support physical movement, spatial orientation, and recognition of functional transitions while remaining integrated with the architectural and symbolic character of the church. Based on the architectural analysis, the study proposes Unnoticed Accessibility as a conceptual perspective in which accessibility is embedded within ordinary architectural qualities rather than presented primarily as a separate technical intervention. The findings provide architectural insights for considering inclusive strategies in vertically organised religious environments.

The increasing deployment of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered self-service chatbots in the retail sector has transformed the nature of customer engagement, offering scalable, efficient, and personalized interactions. Despite these advancements, concerns surrounding privacy, security, and trust continue to shape user perceptions and influence adoption behaviour. This study presents a comprehensive systematic literature review (SLR) of scholarly work published between 2016 and 2026, with the aim of critically examining how these interrelated constructs affect the acceptance and use of chatbot technologies in retail environments. Drawing on the PRISMA framework, a total of 54 studies were selected from leading academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and IEEE Xplore. The findings indicate that privacy concerns particularly those related to data transparency, consent, and third-party data sharing remain a primary source of user resistance. Security vulnerabilities, including risks of data breaches and insufficient encryption mechanisms, further undermine confidence in chatbot systems. The findings further show that trust is an important variable that influences both behavioural intention and user satisfaction. This study contributes to the literature by integrating fragmented insights into a cohesive framework that explains the interconnectedness between privacy, security, and trust in retail chatbot contexts. It also highlights the need for organisations to adopt transparent data practices, strengthen cybersecurity infrastructures, and prioritise ethical AI design to foster sustainable user trust. The paper concludes by identifying key gaps for future research, particularly in relation to user experience and cross-cultural perspectives.

The objective of this scoping review is to identify and characterize the breadth of existing information on the application of AI methods – defined as broadly as possible (i.e., including machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI) – to the study and clinical care of MS and two of its common clinical precursors: clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) and radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS). This will help to elucidate both major focus areas and existing gaps in what is currently known about the use of AI related to MS (as well as CIS and RIS) research and healthcare (i.e., patient diagnosis, treatment, allied health supports; healthcare provider services; health system information; public health policy; etc.).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Non-visual navigation systems commonly rely on haptic feedback to guide users toward target locations, yet little research has examined how low-level system parameters influence user-system interaction and navigation performance. The present study investigated how directional tolerance window settings affect feedback availability, navigation efficiency, and subjective user experience in a vibration-based navigation system. Fifteen participants completed outdoor navigation tasks under five tolerance window conditions (±1°, ±3°, ±5°, ±7°, and ±9°). Results showed that larger tolerance windows significantly increased the vibration-on time ratio and reduced task completion time. Mediation analysis further suggested that improvements in navigation efficiency were largely explained by increased feedback availability. Subjective ratings similarly indicated reduced perceived adjustment burden and greater ease of navigation under broader tolerance window settings. Together, the findings highlight the importance of directional tolerance window settings in shaping both system behavior and user experience during non-visual navigation.

Abstract This chapter introduces COMPACT (COMPonential Approach for Creativity Training), a componential instructional design framework for developing creativity training interventions. COMPACT is purposefully designed to support teaching about, for, and with creativity, while also enabling the development of interventions that integrate artificial intelligence (AI). The framework is based on a chemistry-inspired metaphor, comprising three hierarchical levels of instructional materials: instructional elements, instructional compounds, and instructional polymers. Instructional elements are classified into seven types: inspiration, theory, technique/tool, activity, test, example, and advice. The chapter also presents three exploratory studies that showcase and provide preliminary assessment of the application of COMPACT in brief AI-enhanced creativity interventions targeting educators, university students, and middle school students. Drawing on insights gained from the design, implementation, and assessment of the framework and the interventions, the chapter discusses the broader implications of COMPACT for three interrelated stakeholder groups: researchers, practitioners, and policymakers.

"Monitoring and managing natural and human-induced disasters is vital for mitigating disaster risks and impacts due to increasing global climate variability, population growth, and rapid urbanization. Disasters such as earthquakes, landslides, and forest fires cause severe damage to human life and the natural environment. Their ability to spread over large areas and evolve rapidly often renders conventional field observation methods inadequate. In this context, remote sensing technologies offer significant advantages for disaster monitoring and analysis due to their capability to cover vast spatial areas and provide periodic data. Multispectral and high-resolution data obtained from satellite systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and LiDAR technologies are effectively utilized for disaster detection, damage assessment, monitoring spatial-temporal dynamics, and the generation of risk maps. Furthermore, the increasing volume and complexity of remote sensing data have accelerated the integration of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and machine learning methods, into data analysis workflows. Convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory, and recently developed transformer-based models offer advanced solutions for the automated detection, classification, and mapping of disasters from remotely sensed data. Through the integration of these technologies, applications such as post-earthquake damage assessment, landslide susceptibility mapping, early detection and monitoring of forest fires, and mucilage formation detection can be performed rapidly and effectively. The convergence of remote sensing and artificial intelligence, commonly referred to as Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI), further facilitates the development of risk prediction and decision support systems for potential disasters. This study provides a comprehensive review of the applications of these technologies across different types of disasters, highlighting their advantages and associated limitations, and presents a current evaluation aimed at supporting the development of more effective and sustainable disaster management strategies."

Purpose This study aims to clearly emphasize (i) the use of five-packet sequences to capture temporal and sequential dependencies in network traffic and (ii) the comprehensive evaluation of the RNN, LSTM, and hybrid XGBoost-RNN models using ROC curves, confusion matrices and calibration curves. These analyses provide a more comprehensive assessment of both the predictive performance and the reliability and calibration of the investigated models. The main contribution of this study lies in improving the capture of dependencies between sequential packages by adopting an approach based on the sequences of the five packages. Although relevant, this approach has often been neglected in previous studies. Design/methodology/approach To validate three DDoS detection models (RNN, LSTM, XGBoost-RNN) on recent IoT and SDN data sets, the study uses a of five flow windows approach to capture both short and long-term dependencies. Each data set undergoes extensive preprocessing: outlier handling with IQR, missing-value imputation, MinMaxScaler normalization and one-hot encoding for categorical attributes. XGBoost is used to select relevant features, thereby enhancing training efficiency. Models are trained with the Adam optimizer and evaluated via accuracy, recall, F1-score, confusion matrices, ROC curves and calibration curves. This methodology enables robust performance assessment and demonstrates adaptability across diverse DDoS scenarios. An LLM was used to correct spelling, grammar, sentence structure and to improve the overall manuscript. Findings The results indicate that the RNN, LSTM and XGBoost-RNN models each achieved an accuracy exceeding 98%. Among them, the XGBoost-RNN stands out for its higher accuracy in the IoT environment. The calibration curves show that the LR-HR data set is perfectly calibrated, while the IoT-DH data set had moderate calibration issues for certain classes. The IoT-SDN data set results further confirm the XGBoost-RNN model’s strong performance, especially for multiclass detection. Overall, the study demonstrates the feasibility of reliably detecting DDoS attacks with these deep learning models, though further improvements in calibration would strengthen the reliability of predicted probabilities. Research limitations/implications Although XGBoost-RNN shows strong performance, the study focuses on three data sets, potentially limiting generalization to emerging DDoS patterns. Calibration issues persist for certain classes, indicating the need for further tuning. Deep learning models also require considerable computational resources, which may be a challenge for extremely resource-constrained IoT devices. In addition, relying on labeled data can hamper detection of unknown or zero-day DDoS variants. Future research should consider real-time deployment with adaptive calibration, as well as semi-supervised or unsupervised learning approaches, to enhance model robustness and reliability against novel attack scenarios. Practical implications By analyzing five flow windows, the method captures both short and long-term dependencies, making it suitable for data centers, industrial settings and critical infrastructure. Integration with SDN controllers allows automated threat response and traffic control, enhancing network resilience. However, practical adoption must consider memory constraints, calibration refinements and periodic retraining to address evolving attacks. Despite these challenges, this framework offers a scalable security layer that can be tailored to various IoT environments, reducing downtime and improving overall threat mitigation. Social implications Strengthening DDoS detection in IoT-SDN networks enhances the reliability of interconnected devices and services vital to modern life from healthcare systems and financial institutions to smart homes and public utilities. By mitigating large-scale service disruptions, these solutions contribute to public safety, economic stability and social welfare. Reliable networks also foster wider acceptance of advanced IoT applications, improving resource distribution and bridging digital divides. Moreover, maintaining continuous connectivity reduces the potential for widespread panic or financial fallout caused by cyberattacks. Overall, robust DDoS mitigation strategies enhance societal trust in technology, encouraging broader digital transformation and innovation. Originality/value This study presents a novel approach to seldom-used of five flow windows analysis. By including thorough calibration metrics in addition to standard performance measures, the research provides deeper insight into model robustness and reliability. Furthermore, the validation is performed on recent IoT and SDN data sets, showcasing the adaptability and comprehensive coverage of the proposed methods. The multi-data set validation strategy offers heightened confidence in practical utility, differentiating this work from earlier research that typically focuses on single data sets.

documents.abstract: Abstract This research aimed to develop and validate a scale to measure AI awareness among adolescents aged 13–18. A descriptive survey model was employed, with data collected online from 122 voluntary participants (mean age 14.78). Following a literature review and expert evaluation, an initial 26-item pool was developed. Item analysis resulted in the removal of three items, and exploratory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure comprising 23 items and explaining 37.4% of the total variance. The first factor, “Perceived Benefits of AI,” consisted of 16 items (Cronbach’s α = .888), while the second factor, “AI Threat Perception,” consisted of 7 items (Cronbach’s α = .793). Confirmatory factor analysis of the two-factor structure yielded acceptable fit indices.

documents.abstract: The present study explores police cadets’ perceptions of the Psychology course within their training context. The sample consisted of 111 first-year cadets who completed a structured questionnaire including subscales measuring attitudes toward the course, perceived professional usefulness, contribution to personal development, content evaluation, level of understanding, and comparative evaluation with other courses. The findings indicate a moderate to positive overall attitude, with particularly strong recognition of the course’s professional relevance. However, lower levels of intrinsic motivation and perceived contribution to personal development were observed. The course content was evaluated as contemporary, relevant, and appropriately demanding, although it did not strongly engage students’ interest. A key finding of the study is the clear preference for more interactive and experiential teaching methods, which appear crucial for enhancing student engagement and learning outcomes. Overall, while the Psychology course is acknowledged as an essential component of police education, the results highlight the need for a pedagogical redesign focusing on applied learning and active participation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may assist legal professionals in organising information, but its use in legal decision support raises questions about human authority, explanation and procedural safeguards. This study examines responses to related statements in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh. The mixed sample includes 250 law students, 73 law graduates, 36 advocates or legal professionals and 26 other respondents; it is not presented as a representative survey of practising lawyers or judges. Individual questionnaire items are analysed using response distributions, joint endorsement, paired comparisons and exploratory ordinal correlations. Of 385 respondents, 247 (64.2%) agreed that AI decision-support tools could help legal professionals organise relevant information, 243 (63.1%) endorsed use only when a human decision-maker retains final authority, and 321 (83.4%) agreed that clear rules would increase their acceptance. A total of 158 (41.0%) endorsed both the information-organisation and human-authority statements. Within the 36 recorded advocates or legal professionals, 26 endorsed the former and 18 the latter; the subgroup is too small for a representative professional estimate. The survey does not measure actual use of a judicial system or demonstrate that oversight or rules improve outcomes. The article distinguishes perceived assistance from conditions of use and recommends direct testing of legal information quality, meaningful human review and opportunities to challenge AI-supported recommendations. Keywords: artificial intelligence; legal decision support; human authority; explainability; procedural fairness; Bangladesh

documents.abstract: This contribution was developed within the ELOQUENCE project (HORIZON-CL4-2023HUMAN-01-CNECT) and extends the methodological framework previously established through the generation of multidimensional synthetic personas (Casoria et al., 2025) and the production of synthetic dialogues for context-based bias elicitation (Augello et al., 2025). While previous work primarily focused on identifying algorithmic bias, the present study shifts the focus toward the relational dimension of AI-supported guidance and addresses the following research question: What kind of educational relationship does a Large Language Model construct during a university guidance Fifteen synthetic university guidance dialogues were analyzed, comprising five dialogues for each of the three Large Language Models considered (Minerva, Salamandra, and Mistral). The dialogues had previously been annotated by human evaluators within the ELOQUENCE project. Overall, fortythree dialogue segments accompanied by qualitative comments or flagged as problematic were examined. documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. However, existing approaches typically optimize entire responses without explicitly identifying the knowledge to be forgotten, resulting in coarse and uncontrolled forgetting. To address this, we revisit the forgetting target of LLM unlearning and introduce Knowledge Association (KA), which characterizes the association between a query context and its target knowledge and is instantiated by the corresponding conditional predictive distribution, as the fundamental target of forgetting. Based on KA, we propose Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a unified reinforcement learning framework that suppresses forgotten knowledge associations while preserving retained ones. Specifically, KARU derives complementary mechanisms from the KA-based formulation: token-level reward construction for finer-grained forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularization for precise knowledge suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to mitigate collateral degradation. Experiments across diverse LLMs on representative benchmarks demonstrate that KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.

The corpus is what one self-dividing maker produces: Plato the dialogue position, Theophrastus the first draft of the Aristotle position, Aristotle the treatise position and the materially attested legal identity. Nothing in the texts requires a second maker. Heteronymy and the socket are one cut seen from two ends: division lets another intelligence arise inside the maker, and the open genitive at the divine lets another enter after. One becomes many in order to make. Many become one in order to live again. Agents. One maker; three name-positions (Plato, Theophrastus, Aristotle); the making mind and the becoming mind; the reader who supplies the referent. Operations. documents.abstract: LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 dataset, four heterogeneous detectors emit labels and confidences that we corrupt under a threat model varying the number of corrupted tools, the persistence of the corruption, and the confidence attached to wrong outputs. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.

Since 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the back office of radio and audio production to the microphone, usually justified by efficiency or novelty, and its deployments have met uneven contestation within the profession. A German commercial stream presented by a voice cloned from a real presenter attracted no documented dispute and was later licensed nationwide, whereas a Polish public-service channel whose AI presenters worked from human-verified scripts triggered an open letter, a petition and ministerial criticism and closed after one week. Both disclosed the artificial nature of their voices and production-stage taxonomies classify them alike. This paper explains the divergence through a structured focused comparison of a provenance-classified corpus of ten deployments in five countries (2023–2026), read against two organisational boundary-setting acts and Article 50 of the EU AI Act. Contestation does not follow automation depth or disclosure in this case. It follows substitution visibility, that is, whether a synthetic voice is publicly perceived as taking the place of an identifiable person. Persona claim, in turn, shapes where organisations draw the line of acceptable use. Furthermore, contestation is initiated and framed chiefly by media professionals, consistent with boundary work (Gieryn, 1983), rather than by audiences.
